Star at the center of the [[Solar System]], a G-type main-sequence star (G2V) and the main source of energy for life on Earth.

The Sun is a massive sphere of hot plasma, heated to incandescence by [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]] reactions in its core, radiating energy from its surface mainly as visible light and infrared radiation, with 10% at ultraviolet energies. It has been an object of veneration in many cultures and a central subject of astronomical research since antiquity. It orbits the [[Galactic Center]] at a distance of 24,000 to 28,000 light-years. Its mean distance from Earth is about 1.496×10⁸ km, or about 8 light-minutes; this distance was used to define the [[Astronomical unit|astronomical unit]] (au), now defined as 149.5978707×10⁶ km.

The Sun is the largest and most massive object in the Solar System. Its diameter is about 1,391,400 km (864,600 mi), around 109 times that of Earth, and its mass is around 330,000 times Earth's, about 99.86% of the system's total. It has an absolute magnitude of +4.83, estimated to be brighter than about 85% of the stars in the Milky Way, most of which are red dwarfs. It has no definite boundary; its radius is measured to the edge of the photosphere, the apparent visible surface. Its oblateness is 8.2×10⁻⁶, or 8 parts per million, making it the natural object closest to a perfect sphere ever observed. The photosphere is 74.9% hydrogen and 23.8% helium by mass; heavier elements account for less than 2%, chiefly oxygen (roughly 1%), carbon (0.3%), neon (0.2%), and iron (0.2%).

The Sun rotates faster at its equator than at its poles, with a period of approximately 25.6 days at the equator and 33.5 days at the poles relative to the stars, and about 28 days at the equator as seen from Earth. The early Sun rotated up to ten times faster; magnetic braking, as its magnetic field interacted with the outflowing [[Solar wind|solar wind]], slowed it.

The Sun formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago from the gravitational collapse of matter within a large [[Molecular cloud|molecular cloud]]; most of the matter gathered in the center, and the rest flattened into a disk that became the Solar System. Every second, its core fuses about 600 billion kg of hydrogen into helium and converts four billion kg of matter into energy. About four to seven billion years from now, as core hydrogen fusion diminishes, the Sun will expand into a [[Red giant|red giant]]. Models suggest it will then shed its outer layers and become a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]], which may glow for perhaps trillions of years before becoming an extremely dense black dwarf. The English word *sun* derives from Old English *sunne*; the adjective *solar* comes from Latin *sol*. The astronomical symbol is ☉.

Largest branch of Islam and the largest religious denomination in the world.

Sunnis hold that [[Muhammad]] appointed no successor and that his closest companion [[Abu Bakr]] (r. 632–634) rightfully succeeded him as caliph of the Muslim community, chosen at the meeting of Saqifa. This contrasts with the view of [[Shia Islam]], which holds that Muhammad appointed [[Ali|Ali ibn Abi Talib]] (r. 656–661) as his successor. Sunnis nonetheless revere Ali, together with Abu Bakr, Umar (r. 634–644), and Uthman (r. 644–656), as the four *rashidun* ("rightly guided" caliphs), and honor the *sahaba*, *tabi'in*, and *tabi al-tabi'in* as the *salaf* (predecessors).

The name derives from *sunnah*, the practices of Muhammad. The Arabic term is pre-Islamic, originally meaning "the right path that has always been followed," and gained political significance after the murder of Uthman. During the second Civil War (680–92) it acquired connotations critical of Shia doctrines. Its use as a short group name is relatively recent; Ibn Taymiyyah probably used it first, and scholars such as Muhammad Rashid Rida later popularized it.

The [[Quran]], together with [[Hadith|hadith]] (especially the Six Books) and *ijma* (scholarly consensus), forms the basis of all traditional Sunni jurisprudence. [[Sharia]] rulings are derived from these sources together with public welfare and juristic discretion, using principles developed by four legal schools: Hanafi, Hanbali, Maliki, and Shafi'i. In creed, the tradition upholds the six pillars of *iman* (faith) and comprises the Ash'ari and Maturidi schools of *kalam* (theology) and the textualist Athari school. Sunni Islam is sometimes called "Orthodox Islam," though some scholars, such as John Burton, argue that there is no such thing as "Orthodox Islam."

Powerful and luminous explosion of a star, occurring in the last evolutionary stages of a massive star or when a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]] undergoes runaway nuclear fusion.

The original object, the progenitor, can collapse to form a [[Neutron star|neutron star]] or [[Black hole|black hole]], or disperse completely into a diffuse nebula with no stellar remnant. Peak optical luminosity can be comparable to that of an entire galaxy before fading over several weeks or months.

Most supernovae are triggered by one of two mechanisms. In the first, a white dwarf re-ignites runaway fusion, thought to follow accretion from a binary companion or a stellar merger. In the second, a massive star's core collapses once radiation pressure no longer balances gravity, classically when the star begins producing iron. Supernovae can expel several solar masses of material at speeds up to several percent of the speed of light, driving a shock wave into the interstellar medium and sweeping up a shell observed as a supernova remnant. They are a major source of heavier elements, from oxygen to rubidium, and of cosmic rays, and may produce gravitational waves.

Supernovae occur in the [[Milky Way]] approximately 1.6 to 4.6 times per century on average, and several thousand are typically seen in distant galaxies every year. The most recent in the Milky Way to be observed were Tycho's Supernova in 1572 and [[Kepler's Supernova]] in 1604, both visible to the naked eye; they were used to argue against the Aristotelian idea of an unchanging universe beyond the Moon and planets. SN 1987A, in the [[Large Magellanic Cloud]], provided the only measurements of astronomical neutrinos other than the Sun's.

Medical specialty that uses manual and instrumental techniques to diagnose or treat pathological conditions, alter bodily functions, reconstruct or alter appearance, or remove unwanted tissues, neoplasms, and foreign bodies.

A surgical procedure is generally one that involves cutting tissue to treat disease or injury, though procedures such as [[Endoscopy|endoscopy]] may count if they use surgical settings, such as sterile fields, anesthesia, or suturing. All surgical procedures are considered invasive and often require postoperative care, sometimes intensive. Most are performed by a surgeon and a surgical assistant within a larger team that typically includes an anaesthetist and nurses. Duration ranges from several minutes to tens of hours.

Surgery is classified by timing (elective, urgent, or emergency), by purpose, and by type of procedure. Purposes include exploratory surgery to aid diagnosis, therapeutic or curative surgery to treat a known condition, [[Bariatric surgery|bariatric surgery]] to assist weight loss, and [[Plastic surgery|plastic surgery]], which comprises cosmetic and reconstructive work. Procedure types include ablation, amputation, bypass, grafting, implantation, repair, and resection.

Evidence of surgery appears in the Edwin Smith Papyrus, an Egyptian text from c. 1600 BC that documents the management of wounds, fractures, and tumors through empirical observation. The first public demonstration of ether [[Anesthesia|anesthesia]] in 1846 enabled prolonged operations, and [[Joseph Lister]]'s antiseptic methods in the 1860s reduced mortality from postoperative sepsis. The first successful human kidney transplant, between identical twins, took place in 1954, and laparoscopic techniques were widely adopted in the 1980s. Contemporary surgery spans over a dozen recognized subspecialties. Surgical-site infections still affect up to 5% of cases despite protocols.

Bantu language of the Atlantic–Congo family, originally spoken by the Swahili people along the East African coast and adjacent islands.

Also called Kiswahili, it is spoken by an estimated 40 million to 200 million people, native and second-language speakers combined; most native speakers live in [[Tanzania]] and [[Kenya]]. The name comes from a plural adjectival form of an [[Arabic]] word meaning "of the coasts." Arabic loanwords date from contact between Arab traders and the Bantu inhabitants of the coast, when Swahili emerged as a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]]. Estimates of the Arabic share of the vocabulary vary, with about 40% commonly cited. Swahili also has loanwords from Portuguese, English, German, and was originally written in Arabic script. The earliest known Swahili documents are letters written in Kilwa in 1711 and sent to the Portuguese of Mozambique.

The dialect Kiunguja, from Zanzibar, became the basis of the modern standard language through missionary and colonial efforts. Missionaries adopted the Latin script in 1844, and the British Inter-Territorial Language Committee formalized Standard Swahili in 1930. Swahili played a role in anticolonial movements, and [[Julius Nyerere]] adopted it as a unifying language during the Tanganyikan independence struggle.

Swahili is one of three official languages (alongside English and French) of the East African Community and the lingua franca of much of the African Great Lakes region and East and Southern Africa. It is a working language of the [[African Union]]. July 7 is observed as Swahili Language Day, declared in 2022.

Self-propulsion of a person through water, usually for recreation, sport, exercise, or survival.

Swimmers move by coordinating limb and body movements to achieve [[Buoyancy|buoyancy]] and hydrodynamic thrust, combining forward thrusting actions of the head and torso with arm strokes and leg kicks. The human body has an average relative density of 0.98 compared with water, so it floats, though buoyancy varies with body composition, lung inflation, muscle and fat content, and the salinity of the water. The density and [[Viscosity|viscosity]] of water create resistance that strokes use for propulsion but that also produces drag, so faster swimmers reduce resistance by holding a horizontal position, rolling the body, and extending the arms.

Four main strokes are used in competition and recreation: the front crawl (freestyle), breaststroke, backstroke, and butterfly. The front crawl is widely regarded as the fastest.

Swimming is consistently among the top public recreational activities, and swimming lessons are compulsory in the educational curriculum in some countries. It offers health benefits, including cardiovascular health, muscle strength, and flexibility, and is low-impact because water supports the body's weight. Risks include panic and exhaustion, which can cause drowning, and exposure to [[Infection|infection]] or hostile aquatic fauna; most facilities employ lifeguards.

Cave paintings from approximately 7000 years ago depict swimming, and organized practice existed in ancient Egypt around 2500 BC. [[Competitive swimming]] gained prominence in 19th-century Europe and has featured in every modern Summer [[Olympic Games]], beginning in 1896. Races cover distances from 50 to 1500 m. American swimmer Michael Phelps holds the record for most Olympic medals, with 28, including 23 golds.

Imperial dynasty of China that ruled from 618 to 907, with an interregnum between 690 and 705.

The Tang followed the [[Sui dynasty]] and preceded the [[Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period]]. Historians generally regard it as a high point of Chinese civilization and a golden age of cosmopolitan culture. Li Yuan, who became Emperor Gaozu, founded it after rebelling against the declining Sui; he declared himself emperor on June 18, 618, on news of the murder of Emperor Yang of Sui. Under early rulers such as Emperor Taizong (r. 626–649), military campaigns extended Tang territory beyond that of the Han dynasty, and the dynasty contested nomadic powers for control of Inner Asia and the trade routes of the [[Silk Road]]. The Tang exerted strong cultural influence on Japan and Korea.

The interregnum began in 690, when [[Wu Zetian]] seized the throne and proclaimed the Wu Zhou dynasty, becoming the only legitimate Chinese female emperor. The [[An Lushan rebellion]] (755–763) devastated the empire and weakened central authority. In the 9th century the rise of regional military governors, the *jiedushi*, undermined civil order, and agrarian rebellions caused mass population loss, displacement, and poverty. Zhu Wen overthrew the dynasty in 907.

The capital Chang'an (present-day [[Xi'an]]) was the world's most populous city for much of the dynasty. Two censuses of the 7th and 8th centuries estimated the empire's population at about 50 million, growing to an estimated 80 million by the end.

The era is traditionally considered the greatest age of Chinese poetry; [[Li Bai]] and [[Du Fu]] lived then, with Wang Wei, contributed to the *Three Hundred Tang Poems*. Woodblock printing developed. Buddhism became a major influence, but in the 840s Emperor Wuzong enacted policies to suppress it.

Country (pop., 2024: 67,462,121) in East Africa, within the African Great Lakes region; officially the United Republic of Tanzania.

It covers 947,300 sq km, including the mainland and the semi-autonomous Zanzibar archipelago of Unguja and Pemba. It borders the Indian Ocean to the east and eight countries, including Uganda, Kenya, and Mozambique. It is the most populous country located entirely south of the equator. Dodoma is the capital; [[Dar es Salaam]], the former capital, retains most government offices and is the largest city, principal port, and commercial center.

In the late 19th century the mainland came under German rule as German East Africa, then under British rule after World War I as Tanganyika, while the Zanzibar Archipelago remained a separate colonial jurisdiction. The two gained independence in 1961 and 1963 and merged on April 26, 1964. The name combines Tanganyika and Zanzibar. The country is a presidential constitutional republic that the Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) has ruled for decades as a de facto one-party state.

The population comprises about 120 ethnic, linguistic, and religious groups, and over 100 languages are spoken. The country has no de jure official language; the national language is [[Swahili]], and English is used in foreign trade, diplomacy, and higher education.

The north-east is mountainous and densely forested and contains [[Mount Kilimanjaro]], Africa's highest mountain at 5,895 m. [[Lake Victoria]], Africa's largest lake, and [[Lake Tanganyika]], its deepest, lie to the north and west. Serengeti National Park hosts an annual wildebeest migration involving over 1.5 million animals, and the country is among the most visited safari destinations. Agriculture employs about two-thirds of the workforce and contributes roughly 25% of GDP; gold mining and tourism are also significant.

Philosophical and religious tradition indigenous to China, emphasizing harmony with the Tao (道); also spelled Daoism.

Translations of *Tao* include "way," "road," "path," and "technique"; in the Taoist sense it is generally understood as an enigmatic process of transformation underlying reality. A common goal of practice is self-cultivation, a more harmonious existence in accord with nature. Taoist ethics emphasize the three treasures of compassion, humility, and frugality, along with effortless action (*wu wei*), naturalness, and simplicity.

The core of Taoist thought crystallized during the early [[Warring States period]] (c. 450–c. 300 BC), when the [[Tao Te Ching]], traditionally credited to [[Laozi]], and the *Zhuangzi* were largely compiled. These are widely regarded as the fundamental texts of Taoist philosophy. Monks assembled the growing body of writings into the *Daozang* canon starting in the 5th century. Early Taoism drew on diverse influences, including [[Confucianism]] and Legalist theories. Chinese usage distinguishes *Daojia*, the philosophical tradition of introspective self-cultivation, from *Daojiao*, religious Taoism with its own scriptures, priestly lineages, and rituals, long intertwined with Chinese folk religion so that the boundary is often blurred. Taoist secret societies precipitated the Yellow Turban Rebellion in the late [[Han dynasty]].

Taoism is often compared with Confucianism, and both combined with [[Buddhism]] after its introduction to China, giving rise by the 6th century to the discourse of the Three Teachings.

Today Taoism is one of five religious doctrines officially recognized by the Chinese government, has official status in Hong Kong and Macau, and is a major religion in Taiwan. It also has adherents throughout Southeast Asia, and in the West has taken forms ranging from historical practice to synthesized new religious movements.

Mandatory financial charge imposed on an individual or legal entity by a governmental organization to support public expenditure or to regulate economic activity.

Taxation transfers wealth from households and businesses to the government. Its effect on economic growth and welfare can be increased (the fiscal multiplier) or decreased (the excess burden of taxation). Critics of high tax burdens argue that they reduce incentives for work, investment, and innovation; supporters of progressive structures argue that they mitigate inequality, while opponents say such structures undermine merit-based incentives. Direct taxes fall on income and wealth, and indirect taxes include value-added and sales taxes. Global tax revenues average around 17% of GDP, while those of OECD members reach 33.9% as of 2023.

The first known system of taxation was in [[Ancient Egypt]] around 3000–2800 BC. The earliest and most widespread forms were the corvée, forced labor provided by peasants too poor to pay otherwise, and the tithe. The Rosetta Stone is itself a decree of Ptolemy V containing tax concessions. In the [[Roman Republic]], taxes of between 1% and 3% of assessed property value were auctioned annually to tax farmers called *publicani*, who paid the revenue in advance and kept what they collected. [[Augustus]] replaced this with a direct system under which each province paid 1% tax on wealth and a flat rate on each adult.

In the 17th century taxation may have reached 15–20% of production in places such as France, the Netherlands, and Scandinavia. Rates rose dramatically in Europe in the 18th and early 19th centuries as war became more expensive and governments more centralized, most sharply in England.
